Despite the brevity of the story, the author successfully develops the main characters, Ilse and Jonas, into complex, "round" characters with rich internal lives and shared history. Ilse initially seems stoic and stubborn, deeply rooted in her routine and grief (pushing her late husband Henning's boots aside with her knee for three years without ever moving them away). However, she undergoes significant emotional growth by the end of the story when she offers those very boots to Jonas, signaling reconciliation and acceptance. Jonas is similarly given depth through small, specific details—his impractical coat, his childhood habit of silently enduring wet feet, and his hesitant posture with the suitcase—which paint a believable picture of an estranged son returning home and feeling out of place. Even Henning, who is deceased, feels like a real person through the lingering sensory details associated with him (the clinking chain he stopped trying to fix, the patched size-42 boots). Finally, the cyclist is appropriately "flat"; as a background figure, he requires no backstory, and his brief interaction naturally grounds the setting and establishes Ilse's daily reality rather than feeling like a contrived plot device.
